thread.title: Can the bull market survive without tech-sector leadership?

author: William Watts
title: Can the bull market survive without tech-sector leadership?
text:
Some investors think it is finally time for tech stocks to take a back seat. The big question is whether the bull market can continue to chug along without the sector’s leadership.
For some, the bruising suffered by formerly highflying tech stocks in the wake of what’s become known as the Facebook faceplant last week looks a lot like a long-awaited inflection point, heralding a late-cycle shift in leadership on Wall Street.
See: Prepare for the biggest stock-market selloff in months, Morgan Stanley warns
“As the tech sector has come under pressure in recent weeks, consumer discretionary and industrials, two previously unloved sectors, have started to shine. This is a sign that investors could be rotating out of flashy tech and back into vanilla, stalwart stocks like General Electric Co. GE, +2.93% and Walmart Inc. WMT, +0.24% said Kathleen Brooks, research director at Capital Index, in a note.
On top of that, bears argue it could spell rough sailing ahead for the broader market. Others, however, see it as an episode of overdue consolidation that doesn’t spell doom for either the tech sector or the so-called momentum strategies that center on purchasing stocks with high price momentum.
Read: After a decade of wins, the end may be near for one of Wall Street’s best stock trades
‘Catch-up’ or ‘catch-down’? Instead, the backdrop points to a “catch-up” for stock-market laggards rather than a “catch-down” of market leaders, said Keith Parker, equity strategist at UBS, in a Tuesday note. In other words, sectors and stocks that had thus far been unloved, or underloved, may be enjoying a renaissance.
“Sales and [earnings per share] growth that is nearly 2x the market do not point to a sustained ‘catch-down’ of tech/momentum, particularly when buybacks are rising 171% for tech,” Parker said. Instead, the repricing is in line with the typical “post-VIX shock pattern in which value typically performs better at this stage on broad-based growth and momentum stocks consolidate,” he said, referring to the late January-early February spike in the Cboe Volatility Index VIX, -7.99% that was blamed in part for amplifying a selloff that took the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.
A leadership transition has been long awaited by some market watchers, who have been faked out before, including by violent but temporary bouts of rotation in June and December of 2017.
The tech sector stabilized Tuesday after a downdraft that knocked down the S&P 500 SPX, +0.53% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite COMP, +0.65% for three straight sessions. Earnings from iPhone maker Apple Inc. AAPL, +0.82% were due after Tuesday’s closing bell, and could serve to bolster tech names in coming sessions if the juggernaut posts strong results, Brooks said. But despite any such temporary respite, there is a good chance tech has peaked, she said.
Read: Apple earnings: Watch these 4 numbers
Citing the chart below, Brooks said that while the tech and internet-related sector has led market gains all year, the tide appeared to begin turning in the spring.
Capital Index and Bloomberg Fundamental fears Brooks said it might be asking too much for Apple’s earnings to save the tech sector, noting that shares have been lagging behind some of its peers in recent months. She said that dynamic suggests fundamental issues are weighing on tech, including concerns about the sustainability of the business models of companies such as Facebook, Netflix Inc. NFLX, +1.17% and Twitter Inc. TWTR, +2.09% “along with hefty valuations turning off investors who are starting to look at value-based investing strategies” that favor stocks perceived as left behind and fundamentally undervalued.
Beyond concerns about the ability of social-media companies to continue to grow earnings in the face of worries about their ability to safeguard users’ privacy, the U.S.-China trade spat and expectations that U.S. growth will slow next year, offer additional reasons to be bearish on the sector and the market overall, said Oliver Jones, economist at Capital Economics, in a note.
Trade and growth Investors appear worried “about the prospect of China retaliating against U.S. tariffs by making life difficult for U.S. firms operating there,” Jones said. The information technology sector appears particularly vulnerable to this, given some IT firms’ dependence on China, with semiconductor makers the most exposed.
On the growth front, Capital Economics is looking for a sharp slowdown next year that could lead to recession by the end of 2019.
“This is the main reason why we forecast that the S&P 500 will fall sharply over the next 18 months or so. And in these circumstances, we suspect that the relatively cyclical IT sector would fare even worse than the market as a whole,” Jones wrote.
Big shoes to fill Brooks, meanwhile, is skeptical a sectoral rotation away from tech would be a net positive for the overall S&P 500, given the relative size of the tech titans and the impact of their share price moves on the overall equity market.
“Consumer stocks and industrials may not be able to make up the shortfall if tech continues to come under pressure,” she said.
Parker, meanwhile, said solid growth and stable rates should provide support to year-end, but elevated positioning in growth funds could prolong the current rotation. Financials look the most “tactically attractive” among value stocks, while industrials remain the preferred “cyclical catch-up trade,” he said, noting that UBS remains overweight tech, while health care shares remain its “defensive overweight.”
